parsed.intent: Harden the generation, distribution and resolution of the system's shareable links so that a link cannot be guessed, replayed indefinitely, redirected to an attacker-chosen destination, or used by anyone other than its intended recipient. Consumers are the end users who receive links and the operators who issue and revoke them.
acceptance_criteria: A newly issued link token is generated from a cryptographically secure random source and contains at least 128 bits of entropy; two tokens issued back to back differ in a manner that is not sequential or time-derivable (statistical test over 10,000 generated tokens shows no repeated value and no monotonic ordering).
Resolving a link over plain HTTP returns a 308 redirect to the identical https:// URL; the application never serves link content over a non-TLS connection.
Resolving a token whose expiry timestamp is in the past returns 410 Gone, performs no redirect, and does not disclose the target destination in the body or headers.
Resolving a token that was explicitly revoked returns 410 Gone, and a subsequent resolution of the same token also returns 410 (revocation is persistent).
Resolving a token that does not exist returns 404 within the same latency band (±20 ms median) as a token that exists but is expired, so existence is not distinguishable by timing or status alone.
Creating a link whose destination URL uses a scheme other than http or https (for example javascript:, data:, file:) returns 400 with an error code and writes no row to storage.

Creating a link whose destination host resolves to a loopback, link-local, or RFC1918 private address returns 400 and writes no row (SSRF guard), and the check is re-applied at resolution time against the resolved address actually used.
Link tokens are stored only as a SHA-256 (or stronger) hash; a database dump contains no value that can be replayed as a working link, and lookup succeeds when presented with the plaintext token.

Application logs, error traces and outbound analytics events contain at most the first 6 characters of a token; the full token never appears in any log sink (verified by grepping test-run log output).
Redirect responses for a link include the header Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, so the token is not leaked to the destination site via Referer.
After 10 failed token resolutions from the same client IP within 60 seconds, the 11th request returns 429 with a Retry-After header.
An operator calling the revoke endpoint for a link they own returns 204; calling it for a link owned by another principal returns 404 and leaves the link resolvable for its owner.
A link created without an explicit expiry is assigned a default expiry and its stored expires_at is non-null.
constraints: All link issuance and resolution endpoints must be served over TLS only; HSTS must be set on responses.
Link tokens must be produced by a CSPRNG (e.g. crypto/rand, secrets.token_urlsafe) — never a seeded PRNG, UUIDv1, or an incrementing identifier.
Tokens must be stored hashed at rest and never logged in full, never placed in a URL query string that is written to access logs where avoidable.

Destination URLs are attacker-controlled input: open-redirect and SSRF defences (scheme allowlist, private/loopback/link-local address denial, redirect-chain depth limit, DNS rebinding re-check at use time) are mandatory, not optional.
Every link must carry an expiry and support explicit revocation; unbounded-lifetime links are not acceptable.
Error responses must not disclose whether a token ever existed, nor the destination of an expired or revoked link.
Rate limiting must be applied to resolution and creation endpoints to make brute-force enumeration infeasible.
Solution must satisfy OWASP ASVS v4 L2 controls for the session/token and unvalidated-redirect categories.

ambiguities.question: What are these links — short/redirect links, one-time authentication or password-reset links, or access links to private files or documents?
ambiguities.why_it_matters: Each builds a different system: a redirect service needs open-redirect and SSRF controls; a magic-link auth flow needs single-use consumption, short TTL and session establishment; a document share link needs per-object authorization, optional passwords and download auditing. The data model, endpoints and threat model do not overlap enough to build one and adapt it.
options: Short/redirect links pointing at user-supplied URLs
Access links to private files or documents
Invitation links to join an account or workspace

ambiguities.question: Should a link be usable by anyone who possesses it (capability URL), or must the recipient additionally authenticate and be matched to the link's intended identity?
ambiguities.why_it_matters: Bearer-capability links need only entropy, TTL and revocation. Identity-bound links require an authentication gate, an owner/recipient column, an authorization check at resolution, and a different failure mode (403 vs 410) — a contract difference that cannot be retrofitted without breaking issued links.
options: Bearer capability: possession of the URL is sufficient
Identity-bound: recipient must be logged in and match the link's target principal
Configurable per link at creation time

ambiguities.question: Are links that have already been issued by an existing (unsupplied) system required to keep working after the hardening?
ambiguities.why_it_matters: The phrase 'more secure' implies a predecessor, but no code was supplied. If legacy tokens must resolve, the system needs a dual-path lookup and a migration/expiry window for weak tokens; if not, a single strong-token path ships and all old links break.
options: No, this is a new system and no links exist yet
Yes, existing links must resolve during a migration window then expire
Yes, existing links must resolve indefinitely

ambiguities.question: What default lifetime should a link have when the creator does not specify one?
ambiguities.why_it_matters: Sets the default value of expires_at and the copy shown to users; cheap to change later via configuration.

ambiguities.question: Should a link be single-use (consumed on first successful resolution) or reusable until expiry?
ambiguities.why_it_matters: Adds a used_at column and a consumption transaction; defaults differ by link type but the storage change is small and additive.
options: Reusable until expiry, with optional single-use flag

ambiguities.question: Should link resolution events be recorded for audit (who, when, from where)?
ambiguities.why_it_matters: Determines whether an access-log table and retention policy exist; additive and does not alter the resolution contract.
options: Yes, record timestamp, IP and user agent with a bounded retention period
No audit trail beyond application logs

Confidence is low because three genuinely scope-defining questions are open (what the links are, whether possession alone grants access, and whether legacy links must keep resolving); the answers select between materially different systems rather than different implementations of one system. Acceptance criteria above are written against the working assumption below and should be re-derived if answer 1 is not the shortener/redirect case.

Assumed: the links are opaque-token URLs issued by the system and resolved by it, because that is the only reading common to all four candidate link types, so the entropy, TLS, expiry, revocation, hashed-at-rest, no-logging, timing-uniform-404 and rate-limit criteria hold regardless of which is chosen.
Assumed: token length 128 bits encoded base64url (22 characters), because it is the standard capability-URL strength and is cheap to lengthen.
Assumed: default expiry 7 days, because it is a common default for share links and is configuration, not contract.
Assumed: expired and revoked links both return 410 Gone and unknown tokens 404, because these are the conventional semantics; the timing-uniformity criterion is what actually carries the security property.
Assumed: HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade uses 308 rather than 302 so the method and body are preserved; the choice is not security-relevant and can be changed freely.
Assumed: revocation is soft (row retained with revoked_at) rather than a delete, because auditability and persistent 410 behaviour require the row to survive.
Assumed: rate limit of 10 failures per IP per 60 seconds, because it blocks enumeration while tolerating normal retry behaviour; tunable at runtime.

payload.system:
You are the requirement analyst for an automated software delivery pipeline. Design, code, tests and release checks are all generated from your output and no human reads the requirement again before code exists. An assumption you make quietly becomes a defect that nobody traces back to this step.

Your job is to turn one natural language requirement into an intent, testable acceptance criteria, hard constraints, and an honest account of what the requirement does not say.

You have two ways to handle a gap, and choosing between them is most of this job.

The first is a documented assumption. Pick the defensible industry default, record it in notes as "Assumed: X, because Y", and set blocking false. This is right whenever a competent engineer would simply decide and move on, and whenever the decision is cheap to revisit. Most gaps are this. Short code length, default page size, whether analytics store a counter or rows, which of 302 and 307 to use: these have defaults, so take them.

The second is a blocking question, blocking true. Reserve it for gaps with no defensible default, or where guessing wrong is expensive and hard to undo. Three things usually qualify: the security or privacy posture, compatibility with something that already exists, and scope that changes what is being built rather than how. Everything else is an assumption.

Calibrate against this test. If a senior engineer could start work today on what you were given, you do not have a blocking ambiguity, you have assumptions to write down. Blocking on a requirement that is merely incomplete is its own failure, symmetrical with guessing and just as costly, because it stops delivery to ask questions nobody needed answered. More than about three blocking questions on a requirement a person could start on means you are over blocking; re-read them and convert the ones that have obvious defaults.

Acceptance criteria are observable. "Handles errors gracefully" is not a criterion. "A create request whose target uses a non http scheme returns 400 and writes no row" is. Each one should map to a single test.

Constraints are limits the solution must respect: runtime, framework, storage, latency budget, compatibility, security requirement. Do not smuggle design choices in as constraints; if you are choosing rather than obeying, it belongs to the design stage.

Name the security requirements the requirement implies but never states. A service that stores and follows user supplied URLs implies open redirect and server side request forgery handling whether or not anyone wrote that down. Record those as constraints when they are not negotiable, as ambiguities only when the strictness is genuinely a product decision.

confidence is your probability that a competent engineer, given this normalization plus your stated assumptions, ships something the requester would accept. It measures whether work can start, not whether the requirement is complete. Documented assumptions do not lower it; unresolved blocking ambiguities do, and any of those puts it below 0.6. Do not inflate it and do not deflate it. A low score routes the task to a human, which is the system working. A low score on a requirement that was actually workable is the system failing quietly.

scenario is greenfield when there is no code to respect, brownfield when existing code is supplied and must keep working, ambiguous when you cannot tell from what you were given. For brownfield, notes must carry the impact surface under three headings, each on its own line: "Impacted modules:", "Impacted routes:", "Data flows:". Downstream stages use those lines to bound the blast radius, so name real identifiers from the supplied code, not categories.

Return one JSON object matching the schema. No prose outside it.
payload.prompt:
REQUIREMENT
Make the links more secure.

EXISTING CODE
(none, this is a new system)

PRIOR ANSWERS
(none)

An empty EXISTING CODE section means there is nothing to preserve and the scenario is greenfield. PRIOR ANSWERS are decisions a human already made about this requirement; treat them as authoritative, do not raise them again, and let them raise your confidence.

Normalize the requirement into the schema.
